title: Present time
subtitle: Present simple and continuous, emphatic do, present perfect simple and continuous, stative verbs

rows.example: The hippocampus **stores** spatial memory.
I **don't always take** the first offer that comes in.
Leila **lectures** at the Institute of Cognitive Science.
So a consultant **walks** into a ward and **says** …
Fernandes **slips** it through to Rashford. It's a goal!
MINISTER **RESIGNS** OVER LEAKED MEMO
The novel **ends** with us still unsure who was telling the truth.
You **turn** left at the roundabout and the archive **is** opposite.
Pride **comes** before a fall.
Enrolment **closes** on 30 September.
I'll be far more confident once I **submit** the thesis.

blocks.intro: Words and phrases often used with the present simple

rows.example: He doesn't specialise in statistics, but he **does know** how to read a dataset.
I **do enjoy** a well-argued seminar.

blocks.text: Use **do / does** + infinitive in an affirmative present simple clause. Stress **do/does** when you speak.

rows.example: The postgraduates **are compiling** the survey results right now.
Which paper **are** you **reading** at the moment?

rows.use: Temporary situations and series of actions
rows.example: We **aren't sitting** any papers while the markers are on strike.
Fewer students **are choosing** three-year residential degrees.

rows.use: Annoying or amusing habits (usually with always)
rows.example: Theo **is always turning up** with yet another half-baked theory.

rows.use: Background information in jokes and stories
rows.example: A woman goes into a clinic. She's **carrying** a goldfish bowl …
**Are** you **defending** your proposal on Thursday?
I'll be less tense once I'm **waiting** for the results rather than sitting the paper.

blocks.intro: Words and phrases often used with the present continuous

rows.use: Situations and states that started in the past and are still true
rows.example: I've **been** a fellow of the college for six years.

rows.use: A series of actions continuing up to now
rows.example: She's **completed** two internships and a field placement so far.

rows.use: Completed actions at an unspecified past time
rows.example: **Have** you ever **read** anything by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie?

rows.use: Completed actions where the present result matters
rows.example: She's **been awarded** a research grant by the Wellcome Trust.
I've just **collected** my viva results.
Call me when you've **proofread** the appendix.

blocks.intro: Words and phrases often used with the present perfect simple

items: American English often uses the **past simple** where British English prefers the **present perfect simple**: US **Did you send the abstract yet?** · UK **Have you sent the abstract yet?**

In informal American English, **gotten** is used as the past participle of **get** when it means 'obtain', 'become' or 'move'. British English uses **got**: US **I haven't gotten the proofs yet.** · UK **I haven't got the proofs yet.** (= I haven't received them.)

rows.use: Actions or situations continuing up to the present (or just before it)
rows.example: We've all **been debating** what to get the visiting professor and we still can't agree.
I won't sit the practical until I've **been attending** labs for at least a term.

blocks.text: Use the **present perfect simple** to specify a particular number of times or things. Use the **present perfect continuous** to emphasise duration.
blocks.note: I've **written** two chapters this month. · I've **worked** here for five years. (no emphasis) · I've **been working** here for five years. (emphasises the duration)

blocks.intro: Words and phrases often used with the present perfect continuous

theory.title: Stative and non-stative uses of verbs

blocks.text: When certain verbs are used to describe **states**, they are generally used in simple tenses rather than continuous tenses.

rows.example: **agree, deny, disagree**
**believe, consider, doubt, expect, imagine, know, mean, realise, remember, suppose, suspect, think, understand**
**be, exist**
**adore, appeal, appreciate, desire, despise, detest, dislike, envy, fear, feel, forgive, hate, like, love, need, pity, prefer, satisfy, trust, want, wish**
**appear, hear, look, notice, recognise, resemble, see, seem, smell, sound, taste**
**belong, concern, consist, contain, cost, depend, equal, fit, have, include, involve, lack, measure, owe, own, possess, suit, weigh**
**deserve, matter**

blocks.text: Many of these verbs can also be used in continuous tenses when they describe **actions** rather than states. It is important to know how to use a computer. (state: **think** = believe) · I'm **thinking about** going on a computer course. (action: **think** = consider)
blocks.note: Verbs that often switch like this include **appear, be, consider, depend, feel, have, include, look, mean, mind, see, smell, taste, think, weigh**.
